sourceOfTruth: PHASE3-RESEARCH.md, 2026-08-17. Addenda A, D and E supersede sections 2.5, 2.6, 2.7 and D.6 where they disagree.

evidenceLegend.MACHINE: verified against a real installation on the research machine
evidenceLegend.BINARY: read out of the installed application's own shipped code

clients.name: Claude Code

write.why: ~/.claude.json is the CLI's live state file. It holds oauthAccount, userID and per-project history, is mode 0600, and is rewritten by the app constantly. `claude mcp add` is the only supported programmatic path and the only one that is not a race.

verify.proves: the client started the server and reported that it connected

traps: `claude mcp list` exits 0 even with no servers configured. The exit code is not a signal; the output is.
Leading or trailing whitespace in command, args or env is used verbatim and only warned about.
Workspace trust (v2.1.196+): in an untrusted folder a server stays at `⏸ Pending approval`.
clients.restart: Start a new Claude Code session, or run /mcp in a running one to reconnect.

clients.name: Gemini CLI

write.why: `gemini mcp add` printed `MCP server "nosyparker" added to project settings.` and created no file anywhere on disk. Its own `mcp list` reported no servers immediately afterwards. A hand-written settings.json was read correctly. For this client the usual rule inverts: write the file, verify with the CLI.

verify.proves: the client started the server and reported that it connected

blockers.says: Gemini disables every MCP server, including ones configured for your whole account, in a folder it does not trust. Start gemini in {{cwd}} and run `/permissions trust`, or add "{{cwd}}": "TRUST_FOLDER" to ~/.gemini/trustedFolders.json.

traps: `gemini mcp add` reports success and writes nothing. Never use it to install.
~/.gemini/ is created on first run but settings.json is not written until something writes it.

Folder trust is not announced on startup: gemini opens normally and only mentions it in passing. Both routes out of it were run on a real installation — the `/permissions trust` slash command writes ~/.gemini/trustedFolders.json itself, and writing that file by hand has exactly the same effect. `--skip-trust` is not accepted by the `mcp` subcommand.

clients.name: Codex CLI

write.why: `codex mcp add` created config.toml and wrote the entry verbatim on the research machine. The exact argument order was not recorded there, so the read-back below is what makes this safe: a wrong invocation shows up as a missing entry, not as a green tick. Run against a real installation on 2026-08-18 to answer the one question a CLI-written row cannot answer for itself: it writes the interpreter path through verbatim, with no normalisation, no expansion and no rewriting, so the absolute path we hand it is the absolute path the file ends up holding.

verify.proves: Codex parsed its config, holds our entry, and has it enabled
verify.cannotProve: that the server runs. `codex mcp list` reported a server pointing at /nonexistent/definitely-not-a-binary as `enabled`. It never tries to start the command.

traps: `codex mcp list` is a config read-back, not a health check. It reported a nonexistent binary as enabled.
`enabled = false` in the TOML disables a server without deleting it.
Project-scoped .codex/config.toml is gated behind a trust record in the global config and did not take effect when tested.

clients.name: Goose

write.why: `goose configure` is interactive only; `goose mcp` runs goose's own bundled servers rather than managing external ones. There is no non-interactive add.

verify.proves: Goose parsed config.yaml, our extension is in it, and its own read-back shows it enabled
verify.cannotProve: that the server runs. No session can start without a configured provider, so there is no liveness check here.

traps: The field is `cmd`, not `command`, and `enabled: true` is required — an entry without it never loads.

Malformed YAML makes Goose fall back silently to its built-in defaults: every one of the user's own extensions disappears with no error. This is why the write is a pure insertion and is checked byte for byte afterwards.
`goose doctor` needs a configured provider and exits with an error without one. `goose info -v` does not.

The check used to match the name line alone, which meant two things: a line reporting a problem with our extension confirmed our extension, and the sentence claiming it was `enabled` was never checked against the enable flag it named. It now requires `enabled: true` among that entry's own indented lines, so an entry switched off is a failure and a sibling's flag cannot be read as ours.

clients.name: GitHub Copilot CLI

write.why: The documentation records `copilot mcp add`, but not the arguments it takes, and nothing here has ever been run. The file path and the entry shape are documented, so writing the file invents nothing; guessing an argument order would.

verify.proves: our entry is in the file and the rest of the file is unchanged
verify.cannotProve: that Copilot loads it. Its documentation describes `copilot mcp list` as a health check, and this row asked it until a review pointed out what that was worth: nobody has ever run it, so there was no output to write a pattern against, and the pattern written from guesswork reported success for a line saying the server had failed. It is not asked any more.

traps: `copilot mcp list` is documented and is deliberately not used. A pattern matched against output nobody has seen is not a check, and this one reported `confirmed` against a config file containing nothing at all. If somebody runs the command and records what it prints, this row can have a real check; until then it has none.
Nothing in this row has been run or installed. It is documentation only, and the tier is deliberately one step below what that documentation claims.
The documentation gives one home-relative config path and does not break it down by operating system, so the same path is carried for all three.
The official examples write "type": "local" rather than "stdio", though the documentation says both are accepted. We write what the vendor's own examples write.

This client is not in the community clients.json at all, so the drift watcher can say nothing about it. What is listed there is the Copilot coding agent, which is a web connector with no local config file and a different product.

clients.name: opencode

write.why: It has `opencode mcp add`, but its list command is a real health check, so the file is written here and the CLI is kept for verifying — the same split as Gemini, for a better reason: writing the file ourselves is what lets the entry be checked byte for byte against a schema that refuses unknown fields.

verify.proves: the client started the server and reported that it connected

traps: The entry shape is unlike every other client here. The root key is `mcp`, the type is `local` rather than `stdio`, and `command` is a single array holding the program and its arguments together rather than a string plus an `args` array.
Environment variables go in `environment`, not `env`.
The published schema sets additionalProperties: false, so one extra field is a hard failure rather than something ignored. Nothing may be added to this entry speculatively.
This is the client that proved a bare `node` is not enough: it does not inherit the shell environment, and an entry naming `node` fails with `Connection closed` and nothing else.
The config file allows comments and trailing commas, and its own schema says so.

clients.name: Kiro

extraConfigPaths.says: Kiro's own agent extension reads this file — the path is in its shipped code alongside ~/.kiro/settings/permissions.yaml. We write the surface Kiro's own --add-mcp writes, which is the VS Code one it inherited. Whether the agent also reads that one was not established, so if the entry does not appear in Kiro, this is the file to add it to by hand.

write.why: Kiro is a VS Code fork and ships the same --add-mcp, described in its own --help as adding a server definition to the user profile. Using it means the profile question is answered by the application rather than guessed at.

verify.proves: the entry is in mcp.json after the app's own CLI wrote it
verify.cannotProve: that Kiro loads it, or that its own agent reads this file rather than the other one. There is no list command.

traps: Two configuration surfaces, the second time a VS Code fork with its own agent has had them — Devin was the first. The inherited one is written by --add-mcp; the product's own is ~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json.
The shipped code also references .cursor/mcp.json and .vscode/mcp.json, so Kiro reads other clients' files as VS Code does and the server may appear more than once.
macOS and Windows paths were not established. This client is Linux-only in this table.

clients.name: LM Studio

write.why: Its CLI manages models and the local server, not MCP entries.

verify.proves: our entry is in mcp.json and the rest of the file is unchanged
verify.cannotProve: that LM Studio loads it. It starts a server only when a model actually calls one, so there is nothing to observe until a model is loaded.

traps: The macOS path its documentation gives does not apply here. The path verified on Linux is ~/.lmstudio/mcp.json, and the documented one was not.
The file is created the first time the application is opened, and arrives holding an empty mcpServers object.
macOS and Windows paths were not established from a running installation.

clients.name: Roo Code

write.why: A VS Code extension. There is no command to run.

verify.proves: our entry is in the file and the rest of the file is unchanged
verify.cannotProve: that Roo Code loads it. The extension only starts when its panel is first opened, so there is nothing to check before then.

traps: The file name is mcp_settings.json, read out of the extension's own shipped code, and it lives under the lowercase form of the extension id.
The version number is in the detection path because that is how VS Code names extension directories; the storage directory beside it is the stabler evidence and is checked first.
macOS and Windows paths were not established.

clients.name: Amazon Q Developer CLI

write.why: `q mcp add` exits 0 while refusing to do anything and writing no file, because every one of its MCP subcommands needs an AWS sign-in first. It is the fifth vendor command found reporting success over nothing.

verify.proves: our entry is in the file we were told to write
verify.cannotProve: anything at all about Amazon Q. Every command it offers refuses without an AWS account, no file was ever produced by it to compare against, and the path is from Amazon's documentation rather than from a running installation. This is the least certain row in the table.

traps: `q mcp add` exits 0, refuses, and writes nothing. Its exit code means nothing here.
The configuration path has never been observed on disk: no file was created during testing because every command refused. It is documentation only, inside a row that is otherwise measured.
Every MCP subcommand requires an AWS sign-in, so nothing about this client can be checked without an account.
clients.restart: Start a new q chat session.

clients.name: VS Code

write.why: `--add-mcp` is present in the shipped 1.133.0 build and is the app's own supported write path. It also handles the profile question: a user working in a non-default profile has their mcp.json under profiles/<profileId>/, which a fixed path would miss.

verify.proves: the entry is in mcp.json after the app's own CLI wrote it
verify.cannotProve: that VS Code loads it. There is no `code --list-mcp`, and the enterprise `.policy` variants of the chat.mcp.* settings are invisible from disk.

blockers.says: chat.mcp.enabled is false in VS Code's settings.json: MCP is switched off. Set it to true there, or search `chat.mcp.enabled` in Settings.
chat.mcp.access is not `any` in VS Code's settings.json, so it may refuse a server it did not get from a registry. Set it to `any` there if this server does not appear.
chat.mcp.allowManagedServersOnly is true in VS Code's settings.json, so only managed servers load. Set it to false there, unless your organisation set it.
chat.mcp.deniedServers in VS Code's settings.json lists this server by name. Remove {{name}} from that list.

traps: A non-default profile keeps its own mcp.json under profiles/<profileId>/. Writing the default profile's file alone misses that user; the CLI does not.
The docs contradict each other on whether `type` is required. Writing "type": "stdio" is valid under either reading.
VS Code 1.133 has discovery adapters that read Claude Desktop's, Cursor's and Windsurf's config files. Installing into those clients can register this server in VS Code a second time.

clients.name: Cursor

write.why: `cursor --add-mcp` is present in the shipped build and does write — but not where this row points. Run in a clean HOME on 2026-08-20 it created ~/.config/Cursor/User/settings.json and put the server under `mcp` -> `servers`, which is the VS Code surface Cursor inherited. The earlier note here said it 'exited 0 and created no file anywhere on disk'; that was reached by checking ~/.cursor/mcp.json, the file this row names, which the command genuinely does not touch. Cursor is the third VS Code fork in this table with two surfaces, after Devin and Kiro. We still write ~/.cursor/mcp.json, which is Cursor's own documented user-level config and needs no command; `alsoRemoveFrom` records the other one so uninstall can clean up after that research run and after anybody who has used the command themselves.

verify.proves: our entry is in mcp.json and the rest of the file is unchanged
verify.cannotProve: that Cursor loads it. Its own --add-mcp writes nothing, there is no list command, and where Cursor persists its per-server on/off toggle is unknown.

traps: `cursor --add-mcp` writes Cursor's own user settings file under `mcp` -> `servers`, not the `~/.cursor/mcp.json` this row installs into. On Linux that is `~/.config/Cursor/User/settings.json`, which is where it was measured; the macOS and Windows locations are the standard VS Code ones and have not been watched. Setup writes the file itself; uninstall cleans both. This row used to say the flag wrote nothing, which was measured against the wrong file.
The docs mark `type` as required in this file.
`~/.cursor/` exists on a fresh install but `mcp.json` does not. Installed-with-no-config is the normal first case here, not an error.

alsoRemoveFrom.why: Written by `cursor --add-mcp`, not by us. We never write it, and we remove from it, because an entry we caused to exist is one uninstall has to be able to take away. Only the Linux path was measured — run in a clean HOME on 2026-08-20. The other two are the standard VS Code layout Cursor inherits and are inferred, not seen. Cleaning only ever acts on a file that is there and holds our entry under this key, so an inferred path that is wrong misses rather than damages. Nothing in the output names the platform this was measured on: on a machine we have never looked at, the file is searched for, not found, and nothing is said about it either way.

clients.name: Devin Desktop (formerly Windsurf)

extraConfigPaths.says: This is the file every published document describes. On this build it is not written until Cascade needs it, and `devin.cascade.enabled` is false out of the box. We do not write it; we name it so nobody goes looking for a file we never touched.

write.why: `--add-mcp` exists, exits 0 and prints `Added MCP servers: <name>`. It writes the VS Code-shaped `servers` file at ~/.config/Devin/User/mcp.json, which is the live surface — not the ~/.codeium path the documentation describes.

writeRequiresQuit.says: Devin rewrites its config from memory: a file deleted while it was running reappeared. An entry written now would not survive.

verify.proves: the entry is in mcp.json after the app's own CLI wrote it
verify.cannotProve: that Devin loads it. There is no list command, and Cascade is disabled by default on this build.

blockers.says: chat.mcp.enabled is false in Devin's settings.json: MCP is switched off. Set it to true in ~/.config/Devin/User/settings.json.

traps: Windsurf is now Devin Desktop. Every published document describes ~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json, which is the dormant surface on this build.
Devin rewrites its config from memory: a file deleted while the app was running reappeared. Write only while it is closed.
The bundle carries devin.cascade.readClaudeCodeConfig and strings for Cursor's configs — another route to a duplicate registration.
macOS and Windows paths for the Devin User directory were not established. This client is Linux-only in this table.

clients.name: Claude Desktop

write.why: There is no CLI. `claude mcp add-from-claude-desktop` reads this file, it does not write it, and it is macOS/WSL only.

writeRequiresQuit.says: Claude Desktop rewrites this file wholesale from memory, so an entry written while it is running is lost at its next settings write.

verify.proves: our entry is in the file and the keys that were there before it still are
verify.cannotProve: that Claude Desktop loads it. There is no CLI and no readable state. The only real signal is a per-server log file that appears after the app next starts.

blockers.says: Claude Desktop has an organisation-level extension allowlist configured. Whether it gates a hand-written mcpServers entry or only packaged extensions was never established, so if the server does not appear after a restart, this is the thing to ask whoever administers it about.

traps: The app's config loader falls back to {} on a failed cold-start read and then writes that empty object over the file. A malformed write is not a write that fails; it is a write that destroys the file at the next launch. This is why the entry is read back and re-parsed before anything is claimed.
The app rewrites the file wholesale from memory. An edit made while it is running is clobbered on its next settings write. Close it first.
The file is mode 0600 and sits beside the OAuth token cache. Never log its contents.
clients.restart: Quit Claude Desktop completely and start it again. It reads this file only at startup.

clients.name: Zed

write.why: Zed has no MCP subcommand of any kind. It also leaves a hand-written settings file alone — after several launch and quit cycles the file was byte-identical to what was written.

verify.proves: our entry is in settings.json and the rest of the file is unchanged
verify.cannotProve: that Zed loads it. There is no CLI, the debug log contains no mention of context servers at any level, and there is no state in its database. Zed reports settings problems in its own window and nowhere a program can read.

traps: The file is JSON with comments and Zed's own shipped defaults are wall-to-wall // comments. A parse-and-rewrite would silently delete them, so the edit is a text insertion.
`source: "custom"` is not required. Zed 1.15.0's own embedded example omits it, and an entry carrying a deliberately invalid `source` still started the server. Do not write it.
Zed is installed by a script into ~/.local and is invisible to dpkg and to /usr/share. A detector modelled on the other clients will not see it.
The config directory is created on first launch containing only themes/. Installed with no settings.json is the normal first case.
clients.restart: Quit and reopen Zed. Writing settings.json while Zed was running produced nothing.

clients.name: Kimi Code

write.why: Kimi has no mcp subcommand. MCP is managed only by /mcp-config and /mcp inside the interactive terminal interface.

verify.proves: our entry is in mcp.json and the rest of the file is unchanged
verify.cannotProve: anything about Kimi. It loads no MCP server before sign-in, and every check it offers needs a Moonshot account.

traps: `kimi doctor` printed "All checked config files are valid" while mcp.json contained invalid JSON. It validates config.toml and tui.toml and never reads mcp.json. It is not a check.
Kimi also reads a project-root .mcp.json as a Claude-compatible file, so installing into Claude Code's project scope may register this server in Kimi as well.

clients.name: Cline

write.why: No CLI was found.

verify.proves: our entry is in the file and the rest of the file is unchanged
verify.cannotProve: that Cline loads it. This row is from third-party sources only and was never installed or tested.

traps: This row was never verified against an installation. The path is from third-party write-ups, and only the Linux one was recorded.
Detection here is a directory that only exists once the extension has been installed and run at least once.

Detection was once keyed on ~/.vscode/extensions, which VS Code creates for itself. On a live run `code --add-mcp` created that directory and Cline was then reported as installed on a machine that has never had it. The only evidence now is the extension's own storage directory.

clients.name: Continue

write.why: No CLI was found.

verify.proves: our entry is in the file and the rest of the file is unchanged
verify.cannotProve: that Continue loads it. There is no read-back, and this row was never tested against an installation.

traps: mcpServers here is a YAML list of maps, not an object map. Every other client in this table uses a map.

The docs say edits are not always picked up live and the extension must be reloaded.
